speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Good afternoon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I remain squarely focused on our dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economy has made considerable progress toward our dual-mandate objectives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased substantially while the labor market has remained strong, and that is very good news.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But inflation is still too high, ongoing progress in bringing it down is not assured, and the path forward is uncertain.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are fully committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to achieve a sustainably strong labor market that benefits all.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Today, the FOMC decided to leave our policy interest rate unchanged and to continue to reduce our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Our restrictive stance of monetary policy has been putting downward pressure on economic activity and inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As labor market tightness has eased and progress on inflation has continued, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals are moving into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I will have more to say about monetary policy after briefly reviewing economic developments.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Recent indicators suggest that economic activity has been expanding at a solid pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: GDP growth in the fourth quarter of last year came in at 3.2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: For 2023 as a whole, GDP expanded 3.1 percent, bolstered by strong consumer demand as well as improving supply conditions.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Activity in the housing sector was subdued over the past year, largely reflecting high mortgage rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: High interest rates also appear to have weighed on business fixed investment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our Summary of Economic Projections, Committee participants generally expect GDP growth to slow from last year’s pace, with a median projection of 2.1 percent this year and 2 percent over the next two years.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Participants generally revised up their growth projections since December, reflecting the strength of incoming data, including data on labor supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The labor market remains relatively tight, but supply and demand conditions continue to come into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Over the past three months, payroll job gains averaged 265,000 jobs per month.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The unemployment rate has edged up but remains low at 3.9 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Strong job creation has been accompanied by an increase in the supply of workers, reflecting increases in participation among individuals aged 25 to 54 years and a continued strong pace of immigration.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nominal wage growth has been easing, and job vacancies have declined.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Although the jobs-to-workers gap has narrowed, labor demand still exceeds the supply of available workers.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: FOMC participants expect the rebalancing in the labor market to continue, easing upward pressure on inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median unemployment rate projection in the SEP is 4.0 percent at the end of this year and 4.1 percent at the end of next year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Inflation has eased notably over the past year but remains above our longer-run goal of 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Estimates based on the consumer price index and other data indicate that total PCE prices rose 2.5 percent over the 12 months ending in February and that, excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core PCE prices rose 2.8 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Longer-term inflation expectations appear to remain well anchored, as reflected in a broad range of surveys of households, businesses, and forecasters as well as from measures from financial markets.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The median projection in the SEP for total PCE inflation falls to 2.4 percent this year, 2.2 percent next year, and 2 percent in 2026.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Fed’s monetary policy actions are guided by our mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices for the American people.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: My colleagues and I are acutely aware that high inflation imposes significant hardship as it erodes purchasing power, especially for those least able to meet the higher costs of essentials like food, housing, and transportation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are strongly committed to returning inflation to our 2 percent objective.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee decided at today’s meeting to maintain the target range for the federal funds rate at 5¼ to 5½ percent and to continue the process of significantly reducing our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As labor market tightness has eased and progress on inflation has continued, the risks to achieving our employment and inflation goals are coming into better balance.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We believe that our policy rate is likely at its peak for this tightening cycle and that, if the economy evolves broadly as expected, it will likely be appropriate to begin dialing back policy restraint at some point this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The economic outlook is uncertain, however, and we remain highly attentive to inflation risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We are prepared to maintain the current target range for the federal funds rate for longer, if appropriate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We know that reducing policy restraint too soon or too much could result in a reversal of the progress we have seen on inflation and ultimately require even tighter policy to get inflation back to 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At the same time, reducing policy restraint too late or too little could unduly weaken economic activity and employment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In considering any adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate, the Committee will carefully assess incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The Committee does not expect it will be appropriate to reduce the target range until it has gained greater confidence that inflation is moving sustainably down toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, we’re committed to both sides of our dual mandate, and an unexpected weakening in the labor market could also warrant a policy response.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will continue to make our decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In our SEP, FOMC participants wrote down their individual assessments of an appropriate path for the federal funds rate based on what each participant judges to be the most likely scenario going forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: If the economy evolves as projected, the median participant projects that the appropriate level of the federal funds rate will be 4.6 percent at the end of this year, 3.9 percent at the end of 2025, and 3.1 percent at the end of 2026, still above the medium—median longer-term funds rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: These projections are not a Committee decision or plan; if the economy does not evolve as projected, the path for policy will adjust as appropriate to foster our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Turning to our balance sheet, our securities holdings have declined by nearly $1.5 trillion since the Committee began reducing our portfolio.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: At this meeting, we discussed issues related to slowing the pace of decline in our securities holdings.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: While we did not make any decisions today on this, the general sense of the Committee is that it will be appropriate to slow the pace of runoff fairly soon, consistent with the plans we previously issued.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The decision to slow the pace of runoff does not mean that our balance sheet will ultimately shrink by less than it would otherwise but rather allows us to approach that ultimate level more gradually.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In particular, slowing the pace of runoff will help ensure a smooth transition, reducing the possibility that money markets experience stress and thereby facilitating the ongoing decline in our securities holdings consistent with reaching the appropriate level of ample reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We remain committed to bringing inflation back down to our 2 percent goal and to keeping our longer-term inflation expectations well anchored.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Restoring price stability is essential to set the stage for achieving maximum employment and price stability over the long term.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: To conclude: We understand that our actions affect communities, families, and businesses across the country.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Everything we do is in service to our public mission.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We, at the Fed, will do everything we can to achieve our maximum-employment and price-stability goals.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, it doesn’t—no, it doesn’t mean that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What it means is that, you know, we’ve seen incoming—as I pointed out in my opening remarks, we did mark up our growth forecast and so have many other forecasters, so the economy is performing, performing well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And the inflation data came in a little bit higher is a separate matter, and I think that caused people to write up their inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But nonetheless, we continue to make good progress on bringing inflation down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so— STEVE LIESMAN.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re strongly committed to bringing inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That is—that is our goal, and we will achieve that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Markets believe we will achieve that goal.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And they should believe that, because that’s what—that’s what will happen over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we stress “over time.” And so I think we’re, we’re making projections that do show that happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re committed to that outcome, and we will bring it about.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think there’s some confidence that the market rents—lower market rent increases that we’re seeing will show up in measures of housing services inflation over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s a little bit of uncertainty about when that will happen, but there’s real confidence that they will show up eventually over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, again, uncertainty about the exact timing of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will get aggregate inflation down to 2 percent over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, and I would assume that we’ll continue to see is—we’ll see goods prices coming into a new equilibrium where they’re going down perhaps not as quickly as they had been earlier this year, where housing services inflation will come back down as, as current market rents are suggesting will happen and where nonhousing services will move back down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Some combination of those three things—and it may be different from the combination we had before the pandemic—will be achieved and will bring inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s more—I would put it more in the context of what I said in our—in my opening remarks that the risks are really two-sided here.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We—we’re in a situation where, you know, if we ease—if we ease too much or too soon, we could see inflation come back, and if we ease too late, we could do unnecessary harm to employment and people’s working lives.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so, you know, we do see the risks as two-sided, so it is consequential.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to be careful.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, fortunately, with the economy growing, with the labor market strong, and with inflation coming down, we can approach that question carefully and let the data speak on that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s really what I was thinking.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I want to start by being—saying I always try to be careful about dismissing data that we don’t like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you need to check yourself on that, and I’ll do that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—so I would say the January number, which was very high—the January CPI and PCE numbers were quite high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There’s reason to think that there could be seasonal effects there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, nonetheless, we don’t want to be completely dismissive of it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The February number was high, higher than expectations, but we have it at currently well below 30 basis points core PCE, which is not terribly high.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s not like the January number.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I take the two of them together, and I think they haven’t really changed the overall story, which is that of inflation moving down gradually on a sometimes-bumpy road toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think that story has changed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I also don’t think that those readings added to anyone’s confidence that we’re moving closer to, to that point.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, you know, we didn’t—the last thing I’ll say is we didn’t excessively celebrate the good inflation readings we got in the last seven months of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We didn’t take too much signal out of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What you heard us saying was that we needed to see more that we could, you know—we wanted to be careful about that decision, and we’re not going to overreact, as well, to these two months of data, nor are we going to ignore them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we make decisions meeting by meeting.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we didn’t make any decisions about future meetings today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those are going to depend on our ongoing assessment of the incoming data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I really don’t have anything for you on any specific meeting, looking forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’re pretty modest changes, but you’re right.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There was an uptick in the longer-run rate, and also there’s a 25 basis point increase in ’25 and ’26.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of, are rates going to be higher in the longer run, if that’s really your question, I don’t think we know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think it’s, it’s—we think that rates were generally low during the pre-pandemic post–Global Financial Crisis era for reasons that are mostly, you know, important, slow-moving, large things like demographics and productivity and that sort of thing—things that don’t move quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I don’t think we know.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, my instinct would be that rates will not go back down to the very low levels that we saw, where, all around the world, there were long-run [real interest] rates that were at or below zero in some cases.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t see rates going back down to that level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I think there’s tremendous uncertainty around that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that that higher year-end number reflects the data we’ve seen so far this year because you’re now—you’re now in this year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think that—sorry, say your last part of your question again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I, you know, I think, if you look at the SEP, what it says is that it is still likely in most people’s view that we will achieve that confidence and that there will be rate cuts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s really going to depend on the incoming data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The other thing is, in the second half of the year, you have some pretty low readings, so it might be harder to make progress as you move that 12-month window forward.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Nonetheless, we’re looking for data that confirm the kind of low readings that we had last year and give us a higher degree of confidence that what we saw was really inflation moving sustainably down to 2 percent—toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yeah.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, so, if what we’re getting is a lot of supply and a lot of demand, and that supply is actually feeding demand because workers are getting paid and they’re spending and that’s, you know—what you would have is potentially kind of what you had last year, which is a bigger economy where inflationary pressures are not increasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In fact, they were decreasing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you can have that if you have a continued supply-side activity that we had last year with—both with supply chains and also with, with growth in the size of the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No, not all by itself.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: No.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, we saw—you saw last year very strong hiring and inflation coming down quickly.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We now have a better sense that a big part of that was supply-side healing, particularly with, with growth in the labor force.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, in and of itself, strong job growth is not a reason, you know, for us to be concerned about inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we think—there are many different financial conditions indicators, and you can kind of, you know, see different answers to that question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, ultimately, we do think that financial conditions are weighing on economic activity, and we think you see that in—a great place to see it is in the labor market, where you’ve seen demand cooling off a little bit from the extremely high levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there I would point to job openings, quits, surveys, the hiring rate.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Things like that are really demand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There are also supply-side things happening, but I think those are demand-side things happening.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we saw—that’s been a question for a while.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We did see progress on inflation last year—significant progress, despite financial conditions sometimes being tighter, sometimes looser.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I see the Committee looking at the two months of data and asking the same question you’re asking and saying we’re just going to have to see what the data show.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: As I mentioned, you can look at January, which is a very high reading and you can—and I think many people did see the possibility of seasonal adjustment problems there.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, again, you don’t want to—you’ve got to be careful about dismissing the parts of the data that you don’t like.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So then February wasn’t, wasn’t as high, but it was higher.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we tend to see a little bit stronger—this is in the data—a little bit stronger inflation in the first half of the year, a little bit less strong later in the year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to—we’re going to let the data show.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t think we really know whether this is a bump on the road or something more.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll have to find out.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In the meantime, the economy is strong, the labor market is strong, inflation has come way down, and that gives us the ability to approach this question carefully and feel more confident that inflation is moving down sustainably at 2 percent when we take that step to begin dialing back our restrictive policy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It certainly hasn’t improved our confidence—it hasn’t raised anyone’s confidence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But I would say that the story is really essentially the same and that is of inflation coming down gradually toward 2 percent on a sometimes-bumpy path, as I mentioned.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that’s what you still see.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve got nine months of 2½ percent inflation now, and we’ve had two months of kind of bumpy inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We were saying that we’ll—it’s going to be a bumpy ride.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We consistently said that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we just don’t—we can’t know that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s why we are approaching this question carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It is very important for everyone that we serve that we do get inflation sustainably down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think the historical record, it’s—every situation is different, but the historical record is that you need to approach that question carefully and try to get it right the first time and not have to come back and raise rates again perhaps if you cut inappropriately—prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Have they—well, first of all, I respect our—you know, in our system of government, it is Congress that has oversight responsibility over the Fed.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We place a tremendous amount of importance on our engagements with Congress and always treat them with great respect.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In this case, I would say, those are, you know—our mandate is for maximum employment and price stability and the other things that we do, and that’s what we’re trying to accomplish.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re trying to do that in a way that sustains the strong growth we’re seeing, the strong labor market we’re seeing, but allows us to make further progress with inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s how we can best serve the public and leave the other issues, which in many cases are incredibly important, such as those you mentioned, leave those to the people who have responsibility for those.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We receive these letters with respect, and we write careful responses and address concerns.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We listen, again, because we’re talking to the people who, in our system of government, have oversight over our activity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—but at the end of the day, we take that on board, but we have to make our judgments, and we have to “stick to our knitting”—which is maximum employment, price stability, supervise and regulate the banks, work on the payment system: the things that we do.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re a very consensus-oriented organization, and we do try to achieve consensus and, ideally, unanimity.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: People do dissent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s something that happens.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Life goes on, and it’s not a problem.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ve always had dissents.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But—and so I—you know, you respect thoughtful dissents very much.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s like, you may not agree with some arguments, but you really want to understand them.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you may read a book that takes a position that you have long opposed, just to understand [the position of] that book.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I treat dissents with real respect as well.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Yes.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we, of course, monitor—it’s one of our two goal variables.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We all monitor the labor market very, very carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I don’t see those cracks today.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I, you know—we follow all the possible stories that are out there about, about there being cracks, but the overall picture really is a strong labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The extreme imbalances that we saw in the early parts of the pandemic recovery have mostly been resolved.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing high job growth.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing big increases in supply.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You’re seeing strong wage growth, but wage growth is gradually moderating down to more sustainable levels.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In many, many respects, the things are returning more to their state in 2019, which we can think of as normal for this purpose.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s job openings and quits.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those have both—those surveys have both come down.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So the labor market is—it’s in good shape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, you do see things like the low—the low hiring rate, and people have made the argument that if, if layoffs were to increase, that would—that would mean that the net would be fairly quick increases in unemployment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s something we’re watching, but we’re not seeing it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course, initial claims are very, very low and, if anything, have tracked down a little bit.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So—watching it carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Don’t see it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And when I say something—I, I use the term “unexpected” weakening of the labor market.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we do expect the unemployment rate to—the forecast is that it would move up, I think, closer to what we see as the longer-run sustainable level.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s just—that’s just people’s forecast, individual forecasts.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we’re talking about something that’s unexpected.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s where I’ll leave it, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that is what we’re discussing essentially is—and we’re not discussing all the other many other balance sheet issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will discuss those in due course.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But what we’re really looking at is slowing the pace of runoff.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: There isn't much runoff among MBS—in MBS right now, but there is in Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we’re talking about going to a lower pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I don’t want to give you a specific number because we haven’t made a—haven’t had an agreement or decision, but that’s the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we’re looking at.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: In terms of the timing, I said fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to try to be more specific than that, but you get the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The idea is—and this is in our longer-run plans—that we may actually be able to get to a lower level, because we would avoid the kind of frictions that can happen.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Liquidity is not evenly distributed in a system.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And there can be times when, in the aggregate, reserves are ample or even abundant, but not in every part.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And those parts where they’re not ample, there can be stress, and that can cause you to prematurely stop the process to avoid the stress.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then it would be very hard to restart, we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So something like that happened in ’19 perhaps.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re looking at what would be a good time and what would be a good structure, and “fairly soon” is words that we use to mean fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that—our, our longer-run goal is to return to a balance sheet that is mostly Treasuries.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I do expect that, once we’re through this, we’ll come back to the other issues about the composition and the maturity and revisit those issues, but it’s, you know, not urgent right now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to get this, this decision made first and then we can, when the time is right, come back to the other issues.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we’ll be watching carefully.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But one of the reasons we’re slowing down—we will soon enough, fairly soon I should say, slow down—is that we want to avoid any, any kind of that turbulence.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wasn’t thinking particularly about the banking-sector turbulence, but we—and we had some indicators the last time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: This is our second time in doing this, and I think we’re going to be paying a lot of attention to the things that started to happen and that foreshadowed what eventually happened at the end of that tightening cycle where we wound up in a short[-of-]reserves situation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t want to do that again.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And I think now we have a better sense of what are the indicators.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It isn’t—it wasn’t so much in the banking system as it was around, for example, where federal funds are trading relative to the administered rates and where secured rates are relative to the administered rates.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Those sorts of things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We will always be watching the banking system for similar signs, though.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, I think we broadly think that, once [take-up at] the overnight [reverse] repo [facility] stabilizes, either at zero or close to zero, that, as the balance sheet shrinks, we should expect that reserves will decline pretty close to dollar-for-dollar with that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s what we think.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So it’s sort of ironic that, by going slower, you can get farther.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But that’s the idea.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: The idea is that, with a smoother transition, you won’t—you’ll run much less risk of kind of liquidity problems, which can grow into shocks, and which can cause you to stop the process prematurely.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So that’s—in terms of how it ends, we’re going to be monitoring carefully money market conditions and asking ourselves whether they—what they’re telling us about reserves.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Are they—right now, we would characterize them as “abundant,” and what we’re aiming for is “ample” and, you know, which is a little bit less than abundant.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So there isn’t a—you know, there’s not a dollar amount or a percent of GDP or anything like that where we think we have a really pretty clear understanding of that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re going to be looking at what these—what’s happening in money markets, in particular—a bunch of different indicators, including the ones I mentioned, to tell us when we’re getting close.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then, though, you reach a point ultimately where you stop allowing the balance sheet to run off and you—but then, from that point, there’s another period in which nonreserves—nonreserve liabilities grow organically, like currency, and that also shrinks the reserves at a very slow pace.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So you have a, you know, a slower pace of runoff, which we’ll have fairly soon.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Then you have another time where you effectively hold the balance sheet constant and allow nonreserve liabilities to expand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And then that ultimately brings you, ideally, in for—brings it into a nice, easy landing at a level that is above—you know, above what we think the lowest possible ample number would be.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re not trying for that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want to have a cushion, a buffer, because we know that demand for reserves can be very volatile.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And we don’t want to, again, find ourselves in a situation where there aren’t reserves, and we have to turn around and buy assets and put reserves back in the banking system the way we did in 2019 and ’20.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: MICHELLE SMITH: Nancy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re—most importantly, we’re looking at the incoming inflation data and the contents of it and what they’re telling us, so that’ll be—and also the various components—so obviously that’s what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We want more confidence that inflation is coming down sustainably toward 2 percent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And, I mean, of course we’ll also be looking at all the other things that are happening in the economy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’ll look at the totality of the data, including everything essentially as we make that assessment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But the most important thing will be the inflation data coming in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Wages is one thing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t—our target is not wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It’s really inflation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we would look to the fact that wages are still coming in very strong.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But, but they’ve been—wage increases, that’s to say—wage increases have been quite strong, but they’re, they’re gradually coming down to levels that are more sustainable over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that’s what we want.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t think that—the inflation was not originally caused—we think, I don’t think, by mostly by wages.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That wasn’t really the story.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But we do think that, to get inflation back down to 2 percent sustainably, we’d like to see, you know, continuing gradual movement of wage increases at still high levels but back down to levels that are more sustainable over time.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I guess I’d put it this way: The—if you look at the incoming inflation data that we’ve had for January and February, I think very broadly that suggests that we were right to wait until we’re more confident.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, I think—I didn’t hear anyone dismissing it as not information that we should look at or anything like that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think, generally speaking, it does go in the direction of saying, yes, it’s appropriate for us to be careful as we approach this question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think we’ve been pretty transparent on this, but I will—I’ll try harder.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we are not getting ready to—we haven’t proposed—we haven’t come to a conclusion that we should propose, or anything like that, that Congress consider legislation to authorize a digital dollar.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And it would take legislation by Congress signed by the President to give us the ability to do what we think of as a CBDC, which is really a retail CBDC with the public.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we’re just a long, long way from that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: What we are doing, and I think what every major central bank is doing, is we’re trying to stay in the frontiers of what’s going on in digital finance, and it has many, many different areas.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: It has applications in wholesale finance, in the payment system, and so we need—to serve the public—these issues have become very front burner in the last five or six years—we need to be knowledgeable about all that.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So we actually do have people trying to understand things that are—but it’s wrong to say that we’re working on a CBDC and that we’ve secretly got a lab here where we’ve got one, and we’re just going to spring it on Congress at the right moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We don’t.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I haven’t at all, in my own mind, made a decision that I think this is something the U.S. should be doing.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I just think it’s something we need to be—we need to understand.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We do have people who are keeping up with that, as part of the broader payments landscape.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: That’s, that’s how I would characterize it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I generally think—I mean, this movement actually started 30 years ago—30 years ago, when some academics posited that a more transparent central bank, if the public understands your reaction function, the markets will do your work for you.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: They’ll react to the data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so it all happens that way and so there’s been a march toward greater and greater transparency.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And that—certainly Chairman Bernanke advanced that, Chairman Greenspan did, Chair Yellen did, and I.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, so we went from four press conferences a year to eight, so now every meeting really is “live” now.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think that’s a good innovation.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I wouldn’t want to turn it back.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We also have done a bunch of other things.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: You know, we have an annual supervision report, Financial Stability Report.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I mean, there’s a long list of things that we’ve done.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: I think you—I mean, nothing comes to mind as really desperately in need of doing at this moment.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We’re very transparent.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We have no shortage of FOMC participants speaking to the public through the media.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And so that channel is full, I would say.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So I think it’s generally broadly helped and made things better.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: But not every day and in every way.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Of course not.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: [Laughter] MICHELLE SMITH.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Let’s go to Jennifer, for the last question.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Well, we’ll just have to see how the data come in.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We would, of course, love to get great inflation data.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We got really good inflation data on the second—in the second part of last year.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Again, we didn’t overreact to it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: We said we needed to see more, and we said it would be bumpy.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: And now we have January and February, which I’ve talked about a couple of times.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: So, you know, we’re looking for more good data, and we would certainly welcome it.

speaker: CHAIR POWELL
sentence: Thank you.
